summary: This National Geographic Education article explains economic globalization as the process by which businesses, organizations, and countries operate on an international scale. It traces globalization from ancient trade routes like the Silk Road and the Columbian Exchange to modern communication and trade agreements. It weighs benefits such as lower costs, job creation and reduced poverty against downsides including worker exploitation, unsafe factories, child labor and income inequality.
one_line: A National Geographic lesson on economic globalization's history, benefits such as lower prices and jobs, and downsides such as worker exploitation and inequality.
key_facts: Globalization is defined in economics as the process in which businesses, organizations, and countries begin operating on an international scale.
The Silk Road was an ancient network of trade routes used between Europe, North Africa, East Africa, Central Asia, South Asia, and the Far East.
For more than 1,500 years, Europeans traded glass and manufactured goods for Chinese silk and spices.
The widespread transfer of plants, animals, foods, cultures, and ideas after European exploration of the New World became known as the Columbian Exchange.
The Triangular Trade network carried manufactured goods from Europe to Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, and raw materials back to Europe.
The garment industry in Bangladesh employs an estimated four million people, but the average worker earns less in a month than a U.S. worker earns in a day.
In 2013, a textile factory building in Bangladesh collapsed, killing more than 1,100 workers.
As part of NAFTA, U.S. automobile companies relocated their operations to Mexico, where labor costs are lower.
In Vietnam, globalization contributed to an increase in rice prices, lifting many poor rice farmers out of poverty.
Globalization generally decreases the cost of manufacturing, allowing companies to offer goods at lower prices to consumers.
Studies suggest globalization may contribute to income disparity and inequality between more educated and less educated members of a society.
The relative instability of many African nations is cited by experts as one reason Africa has not benefited from globalization as much as Asia and Latin America.
The rate of globalization has increased in recent years as a result of rapid advancements in communication and transportation.
The article is intended for grades 3 to 12 in Social Studies, Economics, and World History, and was last updated February 20, 2024.
